articles.title: Kushner says Russia is 'comfortable' with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end war after Trump talks with Putin
articles.summary: BERLIN (AP) — U.S. envoy Jared Kushner on Thursday said Russia is "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end the war as it nears the five-year mark. Another American envoy, Steve Witkoff, said U.S. President Donald Trump discussed Ukraine and a peaceful end to the war during his trilateral talks with the Russian and Chinese leaders earlier Thursday.
articles.body: BERLIN (AP) — U.S. envoy Jared Kushner on Thursday said Russia is "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end the war as it nears the five-year mark. Another American envoy, Steve Witkoff, said U.S. President Donald Trump discussed Ukraine and a peaceful end to the war during his trilateral talks with the Russian and Chinese leaders earlier Thursday. Kushner and Witkoff met with European allies in Berlin to discuss their support for Ukraine after a third Ukrainian aerial attack in four days on the key Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Russian-held Crimea halted rail traffic across the span, officials said Thursday, after earlier strikes shut down the road section of the landmark that is a symbol of Moscow's invasion. Train traffic across the bridge stopped after the overnight strike while authorities assessed the damage, but it resumed in the afternoon, according to Russian state news agency RIA Novosti. The Ukrainian strikes seemed calculated to embarrass Russian President Vladimir Putin as he met in China with President Xi Jinping and Trump, as well as to demonstrate that Kyiv still holds cards in the war and to undermine Russia's argument that its victory is inevitable. The attack came hours before the start of talks in Berlin between Kushner, Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alongside more than 40 European leaders who are supporting Ukraine's war effort and fear being sidelined by Trump's direct talks with Putin. The American leader called into the Berlin talks following his meeting with Putin, Kushner said. "We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that," Putin told reporters in Shenzhen, China. He insisted the bridge is a civilian asset, adding that he had ordered the bridge closed to the transport of military hardware or ammunition. Putin also said that the road side of the bridge had been "seriously damaged" but vowed to rebuild it. The rail section is believed to be stronger than the road side, to bear the greater weight of cargo wagons. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The 19-kilometer (12-mile) Kerch Bridge is a key route for military and civilian supplies to Crimea, which Moscow seized in defiance of international law in 2014 and uses to support front-line troops. It is a potent reminder of Russia's illegal annexation of the territory and has been a prime target for Ukraine. A large section of the road deck and an arch collapsed in the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes over seven stages of the operation, according to Zelenskyy, and the train track was damaged by domestically produced Neptune missiles, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said. Now Russia will need to reroute fuel and ammunition supplies over land, where "our drones are waiting for the cargo," the ministry said. The Russian Defense Ministry said Thursday that its air defenses intercepted 53 Ukrainian drones over 10 Russian regions during the night. A Ukrainian attack on Russia's Saratov region killed three people and wounded two others, local Gov. Roman Busargin said, and a drone killed a woman traveling by bicycle with her 8-year-old grandson in the Bryansk region, Gov. Egor Kovalchuk said. Ukrainian authorities said that Russia launched anti-ship missiles and 98 drones at Ukraine, with hits recorded at 18 locations. Explosions and sirens rang out across Kyiv during the day, and the Dutch and Austrian embassies sustained minor damage, officials said. Two people, including a 44-year-old woman, were killed and at least 23 people, including a 12-year-old boy, were reported wounded as Russian strikes caused damage in 12 regions. Russia's bigger army hopes to exhaust Ukraine on the front line through sheer weight of numbers in terms of soldiers, armor and weapons. But Kyiv's defenses are largely holding the Russians back, sapping Russian momentum with the help of drones that quickly choke off troop advances. Russia has resorted to strategic bombing to wear down Ukraine's resistance, placing special emphasis on knocking out power ahead of winter, while Kyiv's domestically developed long-range drones and missiles have struck deep inside Russia, often targeting its oil refineries. In China, Trump called Putin "my friend." The American president's relationship with Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has soured. European leaders have tried to isolate Putin diplomatically and have heavily sanctioned the Russian economy. Ukrainian officials fear their country's fate could be determined by agreements between Trump and Putin, while European governments are alarmed by Moscow's aggression. The question of U.S. support for Ukraine, severely curtailed under Trump, could be raised by Democrats in Congress after their wins in the midterm elections. Britain's Prince Harry offered a veiled criticism of the U.S. government's policy toward Ukraine, saying in an interview released late Wednesday that he believes there is a "big separation" between the Trump administration's stance and that of the American people. Kushner and Witkoff have led Trump administration efforts to end nearly five years of war following Russia's all-out invasion of its neighbor and recently have mediated new discussions, though the talks have yielded no major breakthrough. Kushner said Thursday on X that Washington's priority at Thursday's meeting in Berlin is to "further strengthen our close coordination with Ukraine and Europe, work toward a unified position on the key elements of a lasting peace, and to jointly prepare the agenda and proposed format for the next round of multilateral negotiations." The meeting will also explore how Ukraine's European backers can fit into postwar security arrangements. Kyiv wants to ensure that Russia doesn't invade again, while Moscow wants to keep the NATO military alliance away from its borders. Putin said in Shenzhen that the Kremlin is not against European participation in talks, but "we need to understand with what Europe will come to these negotiations." The Kremlin has proposed to European officials through diplomatic channels to come to Moscow "to determine their position," Putin said, without elaborating. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov declined to say which European officials had been invited or whether Moscow had received a response, Russian state news agency Tass reported.

articles.title: Alleged Russian agent arrested for spying on Silicon Valley tech firm
articles.summary: The company was not named in the indictment but was described as a large, publicly traded technology and defence firm with offices across the US, including in Palo Alto, California.
articles.body: A Russian national has been arrested in California on suspicion of spying on employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defence company that provided support to Ukraine, US officials said on Wednesday.Igor D'iu faces charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, operating as a foreign agent without notifying US authorities, stalking and fraud."Igor D'iu was allegedly recruited, directed, and funded by the Russian government to stalk employees of a major US technology company," Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director of the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, said in a statement.Rozhavsky said D'iu used "physical surveillance, electronic tracking devices, and fraudulent identities to gather intelligence."US Attorney Craig Missakian said the company was targeted because of its "assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia.""We will not tolerate any efforts -- by foreign governments or otherwise -- to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations," Missakian said.What does the indictment say?According to the indictment, D'iu travelled from Turkey to Mexico in June 2026 before being smuggled into the United States, where he allegedly communicated with his Russia-based co-conspirators via Telegram.They allegedly instructed him to gather information on company employees and visit a coffee shop near its Palo Alto office to "photograph their laptop screens while they worked."FBI agents found $18,000 (€15,500) in cash, a fake US passport under the name "Hugo Landry Johns" and two Russian passports during an October raid on D'iu's home in East Palo Alto, according to the Justice Department.If convicted, D'iu faces up to 10 years in prison for acting as an agent of a foreign government without notifying the US attorney general, five years for conspiracy, five years for stalking and one year for fraud.He is scheduled to appear in federal court on 24 November.

Pashinyan says he will ‘step down’ if constitutional change fails
articles.summary: Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said he was ready to stake his political career on the adoption of a new constitution, declaring that he will ‘step down’ if it is not approved. If the new constitution is approved, the Armenian leader said his political mission would be complete so he would not stand in the next elections.
articles.body: Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said he was ready to stake his political career on the adoption of a new constitution, declaring that he will ‘step down’ if it is not approved. If the new constitution is approved, the Armenian leader said his political mission would be complete so he would not stand in the next elections. He ‘guaranteed’ that the adoption of a new constitution would lead to peace with Azerbaijan. Amending Armenia’s constitution is an Azerbaijani precondition for signing a peace treaty, with Baku arguing that the Declaration of Independence, referenced in the constitution’s preamble, contains territorial claims against Azerbaijan. The two countries initialled a peace agreement in August 2025 but have yet to sign it. The newly drafted constitution is expected to be published ‘within days’, Deputy Speaker of Parliament Vahagn Aleksanyan confirmed. The authorities have already stated that the new draft omits the Declaration of Independence — which would meet Baku’s requirements. Pashinyan made the remarks during a Q&A session in Parliament on Wednesday, nearly a week after meeting with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. ‘I believe I can put my entire political capital on the line as a guarantee that, yes, after the adoption of a new constitution, we will have institutional and irreversible peace’, Pashinyan said. Despite winning the June parliamentary elections , Pashinyan’s Civil Contract party lacks the two-thirds majority required to initiate a constitutional referendum and needs support from six opposition MPs to secure the necessary votes. The opposition has vowed to resist the proposed changes and already launched a public awareness campaign against the constitutional amendments, claiming they aim to prevent the adoption of what they call ‘Aliyev’s constitution’. Pashinyan has rejected such wording, and also said he was prepared to ‘step down’ if citizens voted against the new constitution or once the peace agenda he had put forward had been fulfilled. ‘I consider my mission accomplished with the signing and ratification of the peace agreement and the establishment of a fundamental, institutional peace. And I will step down in either scenario’, Pashinyan said. During the Q&A session, Pashinyan also vowed that the government would move ahead with plans to adopt a new constitution regardless of the parliamentary opposition’s position, accusing the opposition of ‘positioning itself as the main obstacle to peace’. ‘We have made a commitment to our people to have a new constitution and to have peace. It would be very unserious if, after some time, we came back and said that because the Strong Armenia faction or the [Armenia Alliance] disagrees with that agenda, we are abandoning it’, Pashinyan said. He outlined two possible scenarios for securing a referendum, describing them as consecutive steps. The first would involve building ‘public pressure’ to force the opposition to abandon its resistance, while the second would involve ‘political developments’ that would result in the opposition groups no longer being represented in parliament. Although Pashinyan did not elaborate on the second scenario, his remarks appeared to suggest his readiness to call for snap elections, which he had previously hinted at. ‘We have enough determination and will to take that path. And secondly, I am convinced that the people of Armenia will turn out for the referendum and vote overwhelmingly in favour of the new constitution’, Pashinyan said. Aram Vardevanyan, the Deputy Parliamentary Speaker from Strong Armenia, said that voters had already expressed their position by denying Civil Contract a constitutional majority in the June elections. In turn, Strong Armenia’s parliamentary leader Narek Karapetyan reiterated that the ‘Aliyev’s constitution’ would not pass, pointing out that the initialled Armenia–Azerbaijan peace agreement contains no provision requiring constitutional amendments. ‘I am offering you the opportunity to remove me. Is this the offer you are refusing? If you refuse, it means you are here for something else. I am telling you directly: if you don’t do it, we will go to snap elections, and you must not be elected; none of you should end up here’, Pashinyan said. In turn, Armenia Alliance MP Kristine Vardanyan, also responded to Pashinyan's remarks. ‘Don’t desperately beg for this referendum. Don’t be so upset that you have failed to present the external demand as a domestic agenda. There will be no deal with you. We will remove you without a deal. The problem is that we don’t trust you or Aliyev; you have given us no reason to believe you’, Vardanyan said. Pashinyan reiterated during a government session on Thursday that he would resign if the proposed constitution was rejected in a referendum. If it were adopted, however, he said he would not run for prime minister in the next parliamentary elections scheduled for 2031, but underscored that his remarks apply only to him personally. articles.title: Armenian Opposition Spurns Pashinian’s Resignation Offer Over Constitutional Referendum
articles.summary: Representatives of the two opposition factions in parliament reiterated their refusal to back a new constitution they say is being pursued by the government at Baku’s behest, dismissing Pashinian’s pledge as a political trap.
articles.body: Representatives of the two opposition factions in parliament reiterated their refusal to back a new constitution they say is being pursued by the government at Baku’s behest, dismissing Pashinian’s pledge as a political trap. Speaking to reporters following a cabinet meeting today, Pashinian repeated a proposal he first unveiled in parliament a day earlier, urging opposition lawmakers to provide the votes needed to put a new draft constitution to a nationwide referendum. Under his terms, he would resign immediately if voters reject the text and decline to seek another term as prime minister in the next general elections if the draft constitution is approved and a peace treaty with Baku is signed and ratified. “I am giving them [the opposition] an unbeatable option, and regardless of the outcome of the referendum, I would be leaving,” Pashinian said. “In one case, having left the peace agenda unfinished, because it turns out that this agenda does not receive the people’s support, at least as presented by me; in the second option, having implemented it in this capacity until the next elections, I will not be a candidate for prime minister in the next elections.” Pashinian warned that rejecting the offer would spell a “political death” for the opposition. Pashinian’s ruling Civil Contract party, which won the June 7 parliamentary elections, lacks the two-thirds majority required in the National Assembly to call a constitutional referendum and needs the backing of at least six opposition deputies. Lawmakers from the two parliamentary opposition factions, Strong Armenia and Hayastan, flatly ruled out any cooperation, stating they do not trust the prime minister and will not vote for what they label “Aliyev’s constitution,” a reference to Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. “By not entering into a deal with Pashinian, we are bypassing the trap set by Pashinian,” Hayastan lawmaker Kristine Vardanian told reporters. “I cannot imagine a scenario in which Pashinian proposes a deal with the real intention of leaving power. Trusting Pashinian’s words would truly be foolish.” Vardanian added that rejecting the offer is not a missed opportunity to oust the prime minister, arguing that “the possibility of removing Pashinian exists everywhere there is no deal with him.” Tigran Abrahamian, secretary of the Strong Armenia faction, echoed that stance, insisting that Armenia’s current constitution is “not subject to bargaining” and that his faction has no trust in Pashinian’s words. Levon Zurabian, deputy chairman of the extra-parliamentary Armenian National Congress, one of dozen opposition groups that recently united to campaign against the constitutional overhaul, also dismissed the prime minister’s proposal, citing what he described as Pashinian’s record of broken promises and alleged fraud in the June 7 parliamentary elections. Writing on Facebook, Zurabian argued that Pashinian should resign first and allow a consensus interim prime minister and a mutually trusted Central Electoral Commission to oversee any vote. He also demanded the release of all arrested activists whom the opposition regards as political prisoners and insisted that any referendum be limited strictly to whether to remove the reference to Armenia’s 1990 Declaration of Independence, the core of the current dispute. The constitutional standoff is central to efforts to finalize a peace treaty between Yerevan and Baku. Although Pashinian and Aliyev initialed a peace agreement during U.S.-brokered talks in Washington in August 2025, Azerbaijan has refused to sign the formal treaty until Armenia changes its constitution. Baku argues that the preamble’s reference to the 1990 Declaration of Independence, which in turn cites a 1989 unification act with Nagorno-Karabakh, constitutes a territorial claim against Azerbaijan and needs to be removed before a peace deal can be signed. Three weeks ago, Pashinian had promised to present the opposition with an offer they “could not reject” alongside guarantees that Azerbaijan would sign the peace treaty and raise no new demands once a new constitution is adopted. Pressed during today’s press briefing by RFE/RL’s Armenian Service on whether he had obtained such guarantees from Aliyev during their meeting on the margins of the European Political Community summit in Dublin last week, Pashinian did not cite any concrete commitments from Baku. “I provide that guarantee primarily with my own political capital – my political credibility,” Pashinian said, adding that while he had discussed the matter with the Azerbaijani leader in Dublin and is working to build broader international understanding, he was putting his own political future on the line. Pashinian confirmed that the preliminary text of the new constitution will be published next week. During his November 19 press briefing, he also stated that he plans to address the nation in the coming days, noting that the speech has not yet been written and will be delivered at the most appropriate time – tailored to how the opposition responds or fails to respond to his proposal. The prime minister warned that if the opposition blocks the referendum in parliament, his government will portray them as an “obstacle to peace” and seek snap parliamentary elections. “We will head for snap elections with this perception [of the opposition], and my gut feeling is that the two current opposition factions will not make it into the next parliament,” Pashinian said.

‘Dignity’ Promised as Serbia’s Parliament Elects New Speaker From Student List
articles.summary: Aleksandar Cupic, a professor and organic farmer who backed Serbia’s student-led protests from the outset, has been elected speaker of parliament following the Student List’s historic election victory.
articles.body: Aleksandar Cupic, an MP from the Student List, was elected Speaker of Serbia’s National Assembly on Thursday as the power handover continued following last month’s momentous elections in Serbia. Members of the Student List applauded Cupic, whilst the majority of the now opposition United Serbia parliamentary group, led by former President Aleksandar Vucic of the Serbian Progressive Party, was absent. Of the 239 MPs who took part in the vote, 97 voted for Stojan Radenovic, while 140 voted for Cupic. In his first address as Speaker, Cupic spoke of his honour on taking the post. “I call on all of you to do everything in our power to restore dignity to the country’s highest legislative body and state institution through lawful means, while also respecting the dignity of every individual MP,” he said. Hew added that voters who had elected them expect all of them to be mindful of every word spoken in the chamber. “That is why dialogue and tolerance must become the foundation of the political culture of each and every one of us,” he said. He added that parliament would foster constructive criticism and oversight, citing Voltaire’s words that “to cease criticism is to be dead”, and stressing that scrutiny makes public officials more serious and accountable. “I promise all of you, as well as all the citizens of this country, that in this role, as in everything I have done in my life, I will be strict and fair. Strict with myself and fair to you,” he added. Cupic addressed the earlier physical attack on the MP Lidija Vukicevic, calling it “irresponsible and inappropriate”, adding that the Student List also condemned it. Vukicevic, a member of the United Serbia parliamentary group, was doused with yoghurt as she entered parliament on Tuesday. The next steps for parliament include electing deputy speakers and other parliamentary officials, while the country moves towards forming a new government, which must be elected within 90 days of parliament’s constitution. Cupic is an assistant professor at the University of Belgrade’s Faculty of Transport and Traffic Engineering, where he has worked for more than two decades. Alongside his academic career, he is an organic farmer, growing fruit and vegetables with his wife on their family farm in Sopot, near Belgrade. A father of six, Cupic entered politics through his involvement in the student-led movement and was nominated for the post of Speaker by the Student List. He has openly supported the student-led movement since the university blockades began in late-2024. He gained wider public attention after hosting hundreds of students on his property during their protest march to the city of Kragujevac. On Tuesday, after 14 years, six parliamentary elections and an equal number of terms of parliament in which Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party and its coalition partners held a majority of seats, the new legislature was constituted. New MPs that day confirmed their mandates and formed parliamentary groups, with Jovo Bakic appointed leader of the Student List group and Aleksandar Vucic heading the United Serbia group, which mostly consists of Serbian Progressive Party MPs. Their respective deputies are Aleksandra Stimac and Milenko Jovanov.

articles.title: Kosovo Ex-President’s Second Sentence Revives Controversy over Hague Court
articles.summary: Already found guilty of war crimes, Hashim Thaci’s second guilty verdict – for attempting to interfere with witnesses – has raised new questions about the court that was set up in The Hague in a bid to avoid such intimidation attempts.
articles.body: This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp Two months after being sentenced for war crimes at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in the Hague, former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci was found guilty of attempting to tamper with prosecution witnesses in the same case. The verdict has brought new controversy for the Specialist Chambers, which has held six trials – three for war crimes, and three for attempts to influence witnesses in the war crimes cases. The court was set up in The Hague in an attempt to avoid witness-tampering, which had been an issue in some Kosovo-related trials at the Yugoslav war crimes tribunal. Thaci was served with an arrest warrant for alleged obstruction of justice in December 2024 while he was already in detention in The Hague. According to the indictment, he tried to influence witnesses at his war crimes trial via allies Fadil Fazliu, Bashkim Smakaj and Isni Kilaj, who visited him at the detention centre in separate visits in July, September and October 2023. articles.title: A new Yalta: How Biden describes Putin, Xi and Trump in his new memoir
articles.summary: The leaders of China, the U.S. and Russia are gathering in Shenzhen for their first-ever formal trilateral summit, a historic meeting that has prompted comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference. The gathering comes just two days after former U.S. President Joe Biden published his memoir, “Promise Me, America.”
articles.body: The leaders of China, the U.S. and Russia are gathering in Shenzhen for their first-ever formal trilateral summit, a historic meeting that has prompted comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference. The gathering comes just two days after former U.S. President Joe Biden published his memoir , «Promise Me, America.» Drawing on personal anecdotes, historical context and his experiences in the Oval Office, Biden offers candid assessments of major international figures and American political leaders. His accounts provide a glimpse into how he viewed some of the world’s most influential figures during his presidency. Let’s look at how he portrays Donald Trump , Vladimir Putin , Xi Jinping and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy . Biden portrays Donald Trump as a deeply divisive political figure whose presidency was marked by confrontational rhetoric, unpredictable behavior and repeated challenges to democratic institutions. Biden is particularly critical of Trump’s refusal to accept the results of the 2020 presidential election and his role in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. He describes Trump’s conduct during the crisis as one of the most serious failures of presidential responsibility in American history. On the international stage, Biden also takes issue with Trump’s approach to traditional U.S. allies and his apparent affinity for authoritarian leaders, including Putin. He recalls how former German Chancellor Angela Merkel expressed frustration with Trump’s behavior and questioned his fascination with politicians who displayed authoritarian tendencies. Biden also criticizes Trump’s handling of the COVID-19 pandemic, arguing that his administration failed to provide the steady leadership and respect for scientific expertise that the crisis demanded. Interestingly, however, the memoir also reveals a more personal side of Trump. Biden recalls being surprised by the warmth of a farewell letter Trump left for him at the White House in January 2021, as well as a cordial conversation between the two after the 2024 presidential election. Biden depicts Russian President Vladimir Putin as a deeply resentful leader whose political outlook is shaped by historical grievances and a desire to restore Russia’s influence. Recalling their face-to-face meetings, Biden pays particular attention to Putin’s personal mannerisms. He writes that the Russian leader liked to «slouch during a meeting, feigning indifference, like a teenager.» Biden also describes Putin’s tendency to arrive late to meetings, interpreting such behavior as a way of projecting power. On the political front, Biden criticizes Putin’s consolidation of power, repression of political opponents and disregard for democratic institutions. He also links the Russian leader’s historical worldview to his decision to launch a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Biden approaches Chinese President Xi Jinping from a somewhat different perspective, portraying him as a powerful leader presiding over China’s growing international influence and increasingly centralized political system. The memoir reflects Biden’s concerns about China’s economic and geopolitical ambitions, including its expanding international infrastructure and trade initiatives under the Belt and Road Initiative. At the same time, Biden describes his dealings with Xi as pragmatic, emphasizing the importance of maintaining diplomatic channels despite fundamental disagreements over human rights, Taiwan and trade. He also expresses concern about China’s increasingly close relationship with Russia. In particular, Biden points to the strategic partnership between Xi and Putin, formalized in their declaration of a «no limits» friendship shortly before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Biden’s account of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy offers an interesting perspective on the transformation of an unconventional political figure into a wartime leader. Before entering politics, Zelenskyy became widely known for playing a fictional Ukrainian president in the television comedy series «Servant of the People.» His background as an actor initially raised questions about his readiness for high-level political office. However, Biden acknowledges that Zelenskyy’s experience in front of an audience proved valuable in his new role. He writes that the Ukrainian leader’s acting background «turned out to be very good training» for the demands of wartime leadership. Biden also recognizes Zelenskyy’s ability to communicate effectively with the public, mobilize international support and rally Ukrainians around their country’s defense following Russia’s full-scale invasion. His personal assessment, however, is not entirely flattering. Biden acknowledges that Zelenskyy could be moody and stubborn during private conversations and was sometimes less appreciative of American support than the former U.S. president had expected.

articles.body: SDA President Bakir Izetbegović met today with ambassadors from European Union member states, led by the Head of the EU Delegation and EU Special Representative in BiH, Luigi Soreca. As stated on Izetbegović’s Facebook profile, they discussed the current political situation in BiH, the implementation of the results of the General Elections, and the formation of government at all levels. They also addressed the priorities and obligations awaiting BiH as it continues its European integration process. Izetbegović emphasized that there is no alternative to BiH’s European path. According to him, the reforms necessary for progress toward EU membership also present an opportunity to strengthen state institutions and the rule of law, improve the business environment, and accelerate economic development. The discussion also covered the SDA’s priorities for the upcoming term. The focus was on concrete reform steps that would accelerate European integration and create the conditions for the formal opening of accession negotiations with the EU. Particular attention, the post notes, was given to stabilizing the political situation, ensuring the functionality of institutions, and creating an environment conducive to implementing key reforms and development projects. In this context, the importance of accelerating the construction of transport and energy infrastructure was highlighted. This is noted as a key prerequisite for attracting investment, fostering a more competitive domestic economy, and creating new jobs. It was also mentioned that this would provide a future for the population—especially young people—encouraging them to remain in BiH.

articles.title: Nine Members of Tashkent Online Drug Gang Sentenced
articles.summary: A Tashkent court has sentenced nine people for running an online drug shop from a prison, with the group’s leader receiving 14 years and one month.
articles.body: Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — A court in Tashkent has sentenced nine people for involvement in a criminal group that organised online drug sales from a prison, the Millar programme on Milliy TV reported. According to the report, the prison’s first deputy governor provided an inmate with a mobile phone. The prisoner then used it to set up an online drug shop. His accomplices outside the prison handled deliveries to customers. Law enforcement agencies detained nine people suspected of involvement in the group during operational activities. The criminal case was heard by the Chilanzar District Criminal Court. The group’s leader was convicted under Article 273, Part 5 of Uzbekistan’s Criminal Code, which covers illegal operations involving narcotic and psychotropic substances for sale, as well as their unlawful distribution. The court sentenced him to 14 years in prison. After partially adding the unserved portion of a previous sentence under Article 60 of the Criminal Code, the final term was set at 14 years and one month. The court also classified him as an especially dangerous recidivist under Article 34. He will serve his sentence in a high-security prison. Six other male members of the group received prison sentences ranging from 10 to 14 years. Two women were also convicted of participating in the criminal group. One had previously been prosecuted and sentenced in 2024. After part of her unserved previous sentence was added, her final term was set at eight years and six months. The court also ordered her to undergo compulsory treatment for drug addiction while serving her sentence.

articles.title: Mikhail Shaidorov parts ways with coach Alexei Urmanov
articles.summary: Kazakhstan’s Minister of Tourism and Sport Yerbol Myrzabossynov confirmed that Olympic champion Mikhail Shaidorov is no longer working with coach Alexei Urmanov. The minister said during a briefing at the Central Communications Service that Shaidorov’s contract with Urmanov had been terminated and that the athlete was now in a new Olympic cycle.
articles.body: Kazakhstan’s Minister of Tourism and Sport Yerbol Myrzabossynov confirmed that Olympic champion Mikhail Shaidorov is no longer working with coach Alexei Urmanov . The minister said during a briefing at the Central Communications Service that Shaidorov’s contract with Urmanov had been terminated and that the athlete was now in a new Olympic cycle. «According to the information available, Mikhail Shaidorov is now in a new Olympic cycle. According to the information available, yes, his contract with Alexei Urmanov has been terminated,» the minister said. Myrzabossynov thanked Urmanov, who won Olympic gold himself and helped develop an Olympic champion. The ministry believes that the coach will continue working with a new generation of Kazakhstani figure skaters. The minister said the athlete was in a new cycle. Since the beginning of the year, he has attended 13 training camps and competed in four or five events. The ministry supports Shaidorov and believes he has the right, as an Olympic champion, to choose a new team and work on new elements. «We have always supported Mikhail. And now, as an Olympic champion, he has the right to choose a new team and work on new elements,» the minister said. Speculation about a possible split between Shaidorov and his coach arose in February, after he returned from the Olympic Games. At the time, media reports suggested that Shaidorov was planning to part ways with Urmanov, who also did not take part in the media scrum. Later, Kazakhstan’s national figure skating head coach Assem Kassanova commented on rumors that the two might end their working relationship. Previously, Shaidorov finished fifth at the third event of the 2026-27 ISU Grand Prix, the Cup of China, in Shenzhen. The Olympic champion scored 263.49 points across the two programs.

articles.title: Kazakhstan may host UFC event within the next two years
articles.summary: Kazakhstan could host a UFC event in 2027 or 2028. The country’s Minister of Tourism and Sport Yerbol Myrzabossynov said negotiations with the promotion are ongoing during a briefing at the Central Communications Service.
articles.body: Kazakhstan could host a UFC event in 2027 or 2028. The country’s Minister of Tourism and Sport Yerbol Myrzabossynov said negotiations with the promotion are ongoing during a briefing at the Central Communications Service. The minister was asked about the prospects of holding a UFC event in Kazakhstan. Myrzabossynov said the parties had been discussing the possibility since the beginning of the year. «We have held several negotiations and working meetings since the beginning of the year regarding a UFC event. By the end of the month, we will provide more details on the decision regarding a UFC event in Kazakhstan in 2027 or 2028. All the work has been completed, and we will announce the results at the end of the month,» he said. The event has not yet been officially confirmed. Its potential venue and host city also remain unknown. The ministry plans to provide further details on the negotiations by the end of November. Previously, UFC CEO Dana White addressed the possibility of holding an event in Kazakhstan. In July, following UFC 329, he responded positively when asked about the prospect. White gave a more specific response on Oct. 25, following UFC 333 in Abu Dhabi. Kazakhstani media also reported a possible visit by UFC representatives to Almaty in November. According to Vesti.kz , a delegation from the promotion reportedly visited the city on Nov. 10 to discuss holding an event in 2027. Neither the UFC nor the Ministry of Tourism and Sport confirmed the reports. Kazakhstan was previously set to host a UFC event in 2020. It was scheduled for June 13 at Astana Arena in Astana, with a bout between Petr Yan and Marlon Moraes planned as the main event. However, the event was canceled amid the COVID-19 pandemic. If the current negotiations result in an agreement, it would mark the first UFC event in Kazakhstan.

UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries
articles.summary: Two sides to commit to discussing third-country hubs as part of reset pact after five-country deal with Rwanda The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document.
articles.body: The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document. A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”. Until now, the Home Office has been seeking bilateral agreements with third countries allowing the removal of migrants, but with no obvious success. Last week, five EU countries – Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands – announced an agreement in principle with Rwanda to establish a migrant “return hub” there in 2027. Burnham hinted at possible cooperation with EU countries last week when he told reporters that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that [the five-country deal] with interest, learning from what went on in the past”. He said: “The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.” The UK has been fighting for deeper cooperation with the EU on migration, with the new deal on a “strategic dialogue” secured in the last two weeks by negotiators in Brussels. It is a key part of the UK-EU reset pact, which also covers a youth mobility scheme, tariffs on Chinese imports, food and drink exports to the EU and a wider restatement of commitment on defence and security. Informed sources confirmed this was the first time the UK and the EU had agreed to “open a dialogue on returns” after the launch of the bloc’s Channel action plan in June this year. Whitehall sources said the UK was now open to the possibility of sending rejected claimants to Rwanda – a recent pivot from the position under Keir Starmer’s government, which rejected the move. According to a draft of the joint agreement, negotiations over third-country hubs will be part of increased cooperation to tackle irregular migration. The document states: “The EU and UK … will establish a structured dialogue on migration covering in particular the joint activities under the Channel action plan, action against irregular migration and migrant smuggling networks, strategic communication and border management, upstream cooperation and engagement with third countries, returns to third countries, pull factors for irregular migrants and legal pathway.” In May, the UK and 45 other European countries signed an agreement that explicitly endorsed plans to send unwanted asylum seekers to third-country hubs. A political declaration from the 46 members of the Council of Europe , the body that oversees the European convention on human rights (ECHR), said states had an “undeniable sovereign right” to control their borders. It is understood that the UK has been seeking a deal with an unnamed third country, similar to the Italy-Albania agreement that allowed Rome to place detention centres in Albania. Albania has ruled out a bilateral agreement on a return hub with the UK. Previous discussions have reportedly centred on 11 countries: Armenia, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, Libya, Mauritania, Rwanda, Senegal, Tunisia, Uganda and Uzbekistan. Montenegro has denied reports that it is considering housing refused asylum seekers. Starmer scrapped a Tory plan to forcibly send small-boat arrivals to Rwanda where their asylum claims would have been processed. Before the election, the Conservative government had spent £700m on its Rwanda returns policy, which was meant to deter Channel crossings. The scheme hit legal and political obstacles from the start, with the UK supreme court eventually ruling it illegal. Under Burnham, the Home Office has refused to close down the possibility of sending asylum seekers to Rwanda. This week, when asked if the UK might ever send asylum seekers to Rwanda, a Home Office spokesperson said: “The UK, like other European countries, is exploring innovative approaches including returns hubs to tackle illegal migration.” The UK has been looking for years to strengthen cooperation with France and other EU member states to tackle small boats carrying asylum seekers across the Channel. But sources say it is only in recent months that there has been a change of mood in the EU, with member states realising that the intensity of criminal trafficking across the Channel is “proving [to be] a pull factor” to enter the EU. Those that fail to make it to British shores remain in the EU’s migrant support system. Responding to the planned cooperation on migrant hubs, Madeleine Sumption, the head of the Migration Observatory at Oxford University, said: “Its inclusion in the statement would confirm the now relatively widespread interest in ‘third country’ options.” In response, Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, said return hubs were likely to be difficult and costly to run. “Removing people to places they have never stepped foot will be difficult and distressing,” he said. “The last decade has shown that working with people to support their return to their countries is far more successful.” A Home Office spokesperson said: “While we are not part of this EU member state initiative, there is widespread international agreement on the need to have practical and workable solutions to deal with the global challenge of illegal migration. “We continue to explore innovative approaches, including returns hubs, to build on the 80,000 people with no right to be in the UK returned or deported since July 2024. We have consistently made clear that we support the principle of returns hubs.”

Uzbekistan Rises to 32nd in UN E-Government Development Ranking
articles.summary: Uzbekistan climbed 31 places to 32nd in the UN’s 2026 e-government ranking, with its development index rising to 0.8930.
articles.body: Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Uzbekistan has climbed to 32nd place among 194 countries in the United Nations E-Government Development Index (EGDI), improving its position by 31 places since 2024, according to the UN E-Government Survey 2026. The report was published by the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UN DESA). Uzbekistan has gained 55 places over six years. It ranked 87th in 2020, 69th in 2022 and 63rd in 2024. The country’s EGDI score rose to 0.8930 from 0.7999 in the previous survey. Uzbekistan is now in the very high EGDI group and belongs to rating class V3. The index comprises three components. Uzbekistan scored 0.8885 for online services, 0.8692 for human capital and 0.9213 for telecommunications infrastructure. Its e-participation index reached 0.8276. Uzbekistan’s overall score was above the global average of 0.6675, the Asian average of 0.7191 and the Central Asian average of 0.7399. The Republic of Korea topped the ranking with a score of 0.9794. The report identifies Central Asia as one of the most notable e-government success stories of 2026. It highlights Uzbekistan’s progress in particular and cites the Digital Uzbekistan 2030 strategy as a foundation for the changes. The UN also assessed online services provided by cities. Tashkent scored 0.8911 in the Local Online Services Index (LOSI), placing it in the very high category. Tashkent received a perfect score of 1.0000 for its institutional framework. It scored 0.9032 for content, 0.9000 for e-literacy and 0.8950 for services. Its infrastructure score was 0.8571, while citizen participation scored 0.8000. The report cites Tashkent’s city portal as an example. It displays five-star ratings for individual services and updates usage statistics four times a day. The Xalq Nazorati platform publishes weekly and annual reports on residents’ satisfaction. Among Central Asian countries, Uzbekistan ranks second only to Kazakhstan. Kazakhstan climbed from 24th to 16th place, with an EGDI score of 0.9363, and entered the highest rating class, VH, for the first time. Almaty led the subregion’s cities with a LOSI score of 0.9604, ranking 12th globally. Kyrgyzstan ranked 83rd with a score of 0.7534, moving from the high to the very high EGDI group. Bishkek placed 55th in the city ranking. The UN highlighted Kyrgyzstan’s Tunduk platform and its cloud-based electronic signature architecture. Tajikistan ranked 131st with an EGDI score of 0.5782, while Dushanbe placed 133rd in the city ranking. Turkmenistan ranked 146th with a score of 0.5388, moving from the middle to the high EGDI group. Ashgabat placed 137th among the cities assessed. The UN E-Government Survey is produced by the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UN DESA). It has been published every two years since 2001. The 2026 edition is the fourteenth and marks 25 years of the assessment. The survey covers 194 countries: the 193 UN member states and, for the first time, the State of Palestine. Its main measure is the E-Government Development Index (EGDI). The EGDI is an equally weighted average of three indices: the Online Service Index, the Telecommunication Infrastructure Index and the Human Capital Index. The Online Service Index is based on an independent review of national government portals and services carried out by UN DESA. Data on connectivity and affordability come from the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), and education data come from UNESCO. Since 2018, the UN has also assessed city portals through the Local Online Service Index (LOSI). The 2026 edition covers 194 cities. The survey’s authors note that the EGDI measures a government’s readiness to deliver digital services. It does not measure how widely people use these services or whether they are satisfied with them. In 2026, 151 of the 194 countries were in the high or very high EGDI groups, up from 138 in 2024. Of the 35 countries that changed groups over the two years, 28 moved up and seven moved down.
